profile.name: Soham
profile.goal: Build durable AI/ML foundations, then explore where careful technical work can be most beneficial.

semester.label: Semester
semester.note: One focused block on class days; 3–5 sessions per week. University overlap counts.

exam.label: Exam
exam.note: Maintenance only. Keep contact with the work; no catching up.

vacation.label: Vacation
vacation.note: Two focused blocks with a real break. Keep one full rest day.

flex.label: Flexible
flex.note: Use the session duration as a guide, not a deadline. Capability gates decide progress.

allowed: Ask for a concept explanation or analogy
Ask for questions that reveal the bug
Request feedback on code you already wrote
Ask for test cases, then write the solution yourself
avoid: Pasting generated code you cannot explain
Letting autocomplete complete the learning objective
Reporting AI output as your proof
Sharing secrets, personal data, or private code
cycle: Write the exact confusion or error
Ask for explanation, not a finished answer
Close the assistant and rebuild from memory
Verify with tests; note what you learned

phases.name: Python Launchpad
phases.summary: Learn to write, debug, test, and ship small Python programs without copying solutions.
phases.promise: You can turn a plain-language problem into a tested Python program and explain your choices.
phases.primary: CS50P — Introduction to Programming with Python
priorities: Python expressions, control flow, functions and data structures
Files, exceptions, modules, classes and tests
Git fundamentals, virtual environments and debugger use
NumPy and plotting as a bridge to data work
stretch: Extra challenge problems after core proof passes

resources.name: CS50P
resources.note: Follow its current weeks and problem sets; if numbering changes, match by topic.
resources.checked: Check current course page before starting

resources.name: Python for Everybody
resources.note: Use only if the primary explanation remains unclear after a second attempt.

resources.name: University of Helsinki Python MOOC
resources.note: Use selected exercises for weak topics, not as a second simultaneous course.

resources.name: Python documentation
resources.note: Use tutorial and library pages to practice reading official documentation.
resources.checked: Version-sensitive; use your installed Python version

resources.name: 3Blue1Brown — Linear Algebra
resources.note: One video when energy permits; math is parallel, not a gate yet.

sessions.title: Tonight: make Python answer you
sessions.outcome: I can run a Python file, change values, and interpret a simple traceback.
steps: Open a terminal and confirm Python with python --version (try py --version on Windows).
Create learning_lab and a file named hello.py.
Print your name, age, and one reason you are learning.
Add two numeric variables and print a formatted sentence with their sum.
Intentionally misspell print, run it, and read the final traceback line before fixing it.
sessions.proof: A hello.py that runs, plus a note naming the error type you created.
checks: Program runs from the terminal
I can point to the file and line in a traceback
I changed the program without a copied solution
sessions.stop: Stop after one clean run and one understood error. Do not install every tool tonight.
sessions.hint: If python is not found, try the Windows py launcher. If neither works, install current Python from python.org and enable Add Python to PATH.

sessions.title: Values, types, and tiny calculations
sessions.outcome: I can choose basic Python types and inspect how values change.
steps: Complete the matching CS50P variables/functions lesson section.
Create budget.py with integer, float, string, and boolean values.
Calculate a weekly learning-time estimate from sessions and minutes.
Use type() to inspect three values; predict each result first.
Write two edge cases: zero sessions and fractional hours.
sessions.proof: budget.py prints a readable estimate for normal and edge-case inputs.
checks: Names describe their values
Predictions match type() output
Zero input does not crash
sessions.stop: Stop when both edge cases run. Formatting polish is optional.
sessions.hint: Print intermediate values if the final number surprises you.

sessions.title: Decisions with conditionals
sessions.outcome: I can express mutually exclusive decisions with if, elif, and else.
steps: Study conditionals in the primary course.
Build pace_adviser.py: accept available minutes and exam status.
Return one calm recommendation: rest, minimum session, or full session.
Test boundaries such as 0, 20, 59, and 60 minutes.
Refactor repeated messages into named variables.
sessions.proof: A pace adviser with a four-row boundary-test note.
checks: Exactly one recommendation appears
Boundary values behave intentionally
I can explain condition order
sessions.stop: Stop once boundary behavior is correct; no graphical interface.
sessions.hint: Evaluate branches top to bottom on paper using one input.

sessions.title: Loops that finish
sessions.outcome: I can use for and while loops without accidental infinite loops.
steps: Study loops in the primary course.
Use a for loop to total seven daily study-minute values.
Use enumerate to print day numbers starting at 1.
Write a countdown with a while loop and state what changes each iteration.
Add an empty-list case.
sessions.proof: weekly_minutes.py plus one sentence explaining why its while loop terminates.
checks: Correct total for a known list
Empty list returns zero
Loop termination is explainable
sessions.stop: Stop after the known-list and empty-list checks pass.
sessions.hint: For while loops, identify start, condition, and update.

sessions.title: Functions with contracts
sessions.outcome: I can split behavior into small functions with inputs, outputs, and clear names.
steps: Study functions and scope.
Refactor pace_adviser.py into recommend(minutes, exam_mode).
Write a docstring stating inputs, return value, and one constraint.
Call the function with at least five cases.
Remove hidden dependence on variables outside the function.
sessions.proof: A reusable recommend function and five explicit examples.
checks: Function returns rather than only prints
Examples cover each branch
Changing a global cannot change the result
sessions.stop: Stop after the function behaves predictably. Type hints are optional.
sessions.hint: Ask: what must the function know, and what should it return?

sessions.title: Lists and dictionaries
sessions.outcome: I can model a small real-world dataset and transform it with lists and dictionaries.
steps: Study lists and dictionaries.
Represent three learning sessions as dictionaries with topic and minutes.
Compute total minutes and topics completed.
Group or filter sessions above a chosen duration.
Handle a missing optional note with dict.get.
sessions.proof: session_report.py prints a useful summary from structured data.
checks: Data and processing are separated
Missing optional note does not crash
I can add a fourth session in one place
sessions.stop: Stop once adding one record updates the report automatically.
sessions.hint: First draw one session record on paper with field names.

sessions.title: Sets, tuples, and comprehensions
sessions.outcome: I can choose between list, set, tuple, and dictionary for a stated reason.
steps: Review collection types and comprehensions.
Deduplicate repeated topic names with a set.
Store an immutable coordinate or date pair as a tuple.
Create a comprehension of completed topic names.
Write a comment explaining each collection choice.
sessions.proof: collections_lab.py with four justified collection choices.
checks: Deduplication works
Comprehension is readable
I can explain why a set is unordered
sessions.stop: Stop after four choices are justified; clever one-liners are not required.
sessions.hint: Prefer the clearest loop if a comprehension becomes hard to say aloud.

sessions.title: Files and durable data
sessions.outcome: I can read and write a small text or CSV file safely.
steps: Study file I/O and with blocks.
Create sessions.csv with a header and three rows.
Read it and calculate total minutes.
Write a summary.txt report.
Test behavior when the input file is missing.
sessions.proof: Input CSV, generated summary, and a clear missing-file message.
checks: Files close via with blocks
Header is not counted as data
Missing file is handled intentionally
sessions.stop: Stop when the report can be regenerated from the CSV.
sessions.hint: Use pathlib.Path to make file paths easier to inspect.

sessions.title: Errors as information
sessions.outcome: I can distinguish syntax, type, value, and file errors and handle only expected failures.
steps: Create one example of four common error categories.
Read each traceback from the bottom upward.
Add narrow exception handling to one input parser.
Avoid a blanket except.
Log the invalid value in a useful message.
sessions.proof: errors_lab.py and a four-line error field guide in README.md.
checks: I name each error category
Only expected exceptions are caught
Unexpected errors remain visible
sessions.stop: Stop after one good and two bad inputs behave clearly.
sessions.hint: Catch the smallest specific exception around the smallest risky line.

sessions.title: Modules and a clean project
sessions.outcome: I can organize code across files and reproduce its environment.
steps: Create a virtual environment and activate it.
Move reusable functions into helpers.py.
Import them from main.py.
Add .gitignore for the environment and cache files.
Write setup/run commands in README.md.
sessions.proof: A small project another person could run from its README.
checks: Imports work from a fresh terminal
Environment folder is ignored
README contains exact run command
sessions.stop: Stop when you can close the terminal, reopen it, and run from instructions.
sessions.hint: Run dir and git status to see what exists and what is tracked.

sessions.title: Classes only where they help
sessions.outcome: I can create a class that protects a useful invariant and know when a dictionary is enough.
steps: Study classes in the primary course.
Create a LearningSession class with topic and non-negative minutes.
Add a readable __str__ method.
Reject invalid negative minutes.
Write three sentences comparing this class to a dictionary.
sessions.proof: learning_session.py with valid and invalid examples.
checks: Invalid state is rejected
String output is useful
I can defend using or not using a class
sessions.stop: Stop after the comparison. Inheritance is stretch work.
sessions.hint: A class earns its place by coupling data with behavior or rules.

sessions.title: Tests before confidence
sessions.outcome: I can write repeatable tests that cover normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
steps: Study pytest or CS50P testing material.
Choose recommend or LearningSession as the unit under test.
Write one normal, one boundary, and one invalid-input test.
Run tests, break the implementation, and observe a failure.
Fix it and record the command in README.
sessions.proof: At least three automated tests with a witnessed fail-then-pass cycle.
checks: All tests pass after the fix
A deliberate bug made a test fail
Tests do not rely on print inspection
sessions.stop: Stop at three meaningful tests; chasing coverage percentage is optional.
sessions.hint: Each test should answer one behavior question.

sessions.title: Debug with evidence
sessions.outcome: I can pause execution, inspect state, and locate a bug without scattering print calls.
steps: Open a prior project in the VS Code debugger.
Set a breakpoint inside a loop or function.
Step over and inspect two changing variables.
Use one conditional breakpoint or watch expression if available.
Write the bug, evidence, and fix in a debug note.
sessions.proof: A short debugging note with symptom → observation → cause → fix.
checks: Breakpoint pauses on the expected line
I inspected live values
Fix follows from observed evidence
sessions.stop: Stop once one real or planted bug is explained.
sessions.hint: Use a deliberately wrong boundary condition if no natural bug exists.

sessions.title: Git as meaningful history
sessions.outcome: I can create a repository, inspect changes, and make coherent commits tied to deliverables.
steps: Initialize Git in the Phase 0 project if needed.
Inspect git status and git diff.
Commit the working project as one meaningful deliverable.
Make a small README improvement and commit it separately.
View the log and explain why the split is useful.
sessions.proof: A local repository with two coherent commits and a clean status.
checks: No secrets or environment folder tracked
Commit messages describe outcomes
I can show the change in each commit
sessions.stop: Stop at a clean local repository. Publishing online is optional.
sessions.hint: Commit when a meaningful unit works—not because a calendar day ended.

sessions.title: NumPy arrays and shapes
sessions.outcome: I can create, index, reshape, and combine arrays while tracking shape.
steps: Install NumPy inside the project environment.
Create 1D and 2D arrays and print shape and dtype.
Select rows, columns, and a slice.
Reshape compatible data and explain why one incompatible reshape fails.
Compute column means.
sessions.proof: numpy_shapes.py with prediction comments before each printed shape.
checks: Shape predictions are correct
Slicing does not confuse rows and columns
Failed reshape is explained by element count
sessions.stop: Stop after column means and shape explanations.
sessions.hint: Write dimensions as rows × columns before running.

sessions.title: Vectorization and broadcasting
sessions.outcome: I can replace a simple Python loop with a vectorized NumPy operation and validate the result.
steps: Normalize a numeric array with a loop.
Implement the same result with NumPy operations.
Use broadcasting to center each column of a matrix.
Compare outputs with np.allclose.
Record shape at every transformation.
sessions.proof: vectorization.py with loop and vectorized versions that agree.
checks: np.allclose is true
Broadcasting dimensions are explainable
No premature performance claims
sessions.stop: Stop when results match; benchmarking is optional.
sessions.hint: Align shapes from the trailing dimensions when reasoning about broadcasting.

sessions.title: Plot a truthful story
sessions.outcome: I can choose a basic chart, label it clearly, and avoid implying more than the data shows.
steps: Install Matplotlib in the environment.
Plot daily minutes as a line or bar chart.
Add title, axis labels, units, and source note.
Create one misleading version, then identify and fix the issue.
Save the final figure to a file.
sessions.proof: A readable PNG and a two-sentence chart interpretation.
checks: Axes and units are labeled
Interpretation matches data
Misleading choice is identified
sessions.stop: Stop after one honest chart. Styling is not the objective.
sessions.hint: Start the y-axis at zero for bars unless you have a stated reason not to.

sessions.title: Phase 0 proof: learning-log CLI
sessions.outcome: I can independently build, test, debug, document, and version a small Python program.
steps: Build a CLI that adds a learning session to a local CSV or JSON file.
Support listing sessions and computing total minutes by topic.
Validate bad or negative input.
Write at least six tests across core behavior.
Use the debugger on one planted defect.
Write a README with setup, use, design choices, and limitations.
Create coherent commits after working deliverables.
sessions.proof: A local learning-log repository with tests, sample data, README, and clean Git history.
checks: A new user can follow the README
Data survives program restart
Invalid input is handled
Six meaningful tests pass
I can explain every function without notes
sessions.stop: Stop when the checkpoint evidence exists. Publishing and extra features are optional.
sessions.hint: Build one vertical slice first: add one session, save it, restart, list it.

gates: Build the learning-log CLI from a blank folder using documentation, not a copied tutorial
Write and pass tests for normal, boundary, and invalid behavior
Read a traceback and use a debugger to locate a planted bug
Explain choices among function, dictionary, class, list, set, and tuple
Create a reproducible environment, README, and coherent Git history
Manipulate NumPy arrays while predicting shapes, then produce one labeled plot

phases.summary: Connect mathematical intuition to a reproducible classical ML workflow on real tabular data.
phases.promise: You can build and critique a leakage-resistant scikit-learn experiment, not merely fit a model.
phases.primary: Kaggle Learn Intro + Intermediate ML, supported by StatQuest and targeted math
priorities: pandas inspection, cleaning, joins, grouping and visualization
Regression/classification metrics, baselines and error analysis
Cross-validation, reproducibility, tests and experiment reports
Linear algebra, calculus, probability and optimization connected to code
stretch: Derive linear regression gradients from scratch
Kaggle competition ranking or extensive tuning
